title: Lalla's two names
hook: Hindus call her Lalleshwari, Muslims Lal Arifa, and a Sufi saint asked God for what she had
tomorrow: a princess turns down her palace's god. who does she choose?

segments.voice: Yesterday, in my own house: Lalla searched far and recognized Shiva at home. Today, the names people gave her afterward, and there's more than one.
screen: `IN MY OWN HOUSE.` → `MORE THAN ONE NAME.`

segments.voice: Sunday lunch at Theo's parents' house. His grandpa called him Teddy all through the meal, his sister called him Theodore, and Zoe, who calls him Theo, almost corrected them both. Afterward, on his own porch, Ray laughed: his students called him three different things, and he answered to all of them. Lalla has more than one name too. Hindus call her Lalleshwari. Muslims call her Lal Arifa. Why both?
screen: `TEDDY, THEODORE, THEO.` → `RAY ANSWERED TO ALL OF THEM.` → `LALLESHWARI. LAL ARIFA.`

segments.voice: Because both communities claim her, and each honored her in its own words of honor. To Kashmiri Hindus she's Lalleshwari, Lalla the Lady, ishwari, a word used for a goddess. To Kashmiri Muslims she's Lal Arifa: in Sufi language an arif is one who knows God directly, not from books. And Kashmiris of both faiths also call her Lal Ded, Granny Lalla. There's a story that ties the names together. Kashmir's Sufi saint Nund Rishi, also called Sheikh Nur-ud-din, founded the order of Rishis, Muslim mystics of the valley. Legend says that as a newborn he wouldn't nurse, until Lalla came and fed him herself. Grown, he's said to have sung of her: that Lalla of Padmanpur drank her fill of the nectar of God; grant me the same, O God. A Sufi saint, praying to receive what a Shaiva yogini had. Here's the teaching. In Kashmir, Lalla stands between two traditions, and neither had to give up its own words to honor her. The Shaiva calls her the Lady; the Sufi calls her the one who knows. The names don't cancel; they each tell you something true about her, and about the people saying them. So the grandpa's Teddy isn't a mistake to fix. It's his word for love, from before Theo chose his own.
screen: `LALLESHWARI: LALLA THE LADY.` · `LAL ARIFA: THE ONE WHO KNOWS GOD.` · `NUND RISHI ASKS FOR WHAT SHE HAD.` · `EACH NAME TELLS SOMETHING TRUE.` · then, large: `TWO NAMES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose name you've heard said more than one way: a nickname, a family name, a name in another language. Say each version out loud, slowly, the way the people who use it say it. Then sit, and hear what each one carries.
Lalla's two names: Lalleshwari to Hindus, Lal Arifa to Muslims, and Lal Ded, Granny Lalla, to both.
Keep this one: two names, and neither one a mistake. Lalla's days are done; Mira's begin next.
